entry: Dramatic literary form of scripted dialogue and monologue, performed by actors before an audience. Performers read or memorize their lines from a script, which is also called a play, and its words are meant to be spoken aloud rather than read silently. Plays are staged at levels from London's West End and New York's Broadway to regional, community and academic theater. Stage plays are written for live performance, although some dramatists, notably [[George Bernard Shaw]], cared little whether their plays were performed or read. The two original genres of [[Ancient Greece|Ancient Greek]] drama were [[Comedy|comedy]] and tragedy. Historical plays center on real events, and satirical plays, such as [[Aristophanes]]'s *Lysistrata*, comment on contemporary politics. [[William Shakespeare]] wrote both comedies, such as *A Midsummer Night's Dream*, and tragedies, such as *Hamlet*.

American men's lifestyle and entertainment magazine, founded in Chicago in 1953 by [[Hugh Hefner]] and associates. Hefner funded it with a US$1,000 loan from his mother, and its first centerfold was [[Marilyn Monroe]]. The magazine was known for centerfolds of nude and semi-nude female models called Playmates. It published interviews with celebrities and politicians, short stories by novelists including [[Arthur C. Clarke]], [[Ian Fleming]] and [[Vladimir Nabokov]], and full-page color cartoons. The magazine played an important role in the [[Sexual revolution]]. Second-wave feminists, including [[Gloria Steinem]], criticized it for commodifying women, while supporters credited it with promoting free speech and civil rights. After a year-long removal of most nude photos, the March–April 2017 issue brought back nudity.

Outdoor area designed for children's play, usually equipped with structures such as slides, swings and seesaws. Modern playgrounds often include merry-go-rounds, jungle gyms, sandboxes and mazes, which help children develop physical coordination and strength as well as social and emotional skills. Some have facilities for informal sports such as a basketball court. A playscape is a playground designed to be safe in a natural setting. In 1843 Thomas Carlyle called for public playgrounds in industrial cities such as [[Manchester]]. The first purpose-built public playgrounds opened in 1846 in Salford and Manchester, England. One of the first in the United States was built in 1887 in [[San Francisco]]'s Golden Gate Park. In post-war London, designers and advocates including Lady Allen of Hurtwood popularized the "junk playground," where children built structures from rubble.

Experience that feels good and involves enjoyment of something, contrasted with [[Pain]] and [[Suffering]]. Pleasure is closely related to value, desire and action, and it plays a central role in hedonism, the family of philosophical theories that treat it as the good. Pleasurable experiences include eating, having sex, listening to [[Music|music]], seeing a [[Sunset|sunset]] and playing games. [[Epicurus]] identified pleasure, defined as the absence of pain in the body and disturbance in the soul, as the highest good. [[Jeremy Bentham]] listed 14 kinds of pleasure, including sense, wealth, skill and memory. Neuroscience links pleasure to reward circuits in the brain, where dopamine signals anticipation and opioids support the experience of liking. Pleasure is not identical to [[Happiness]] or well-being, although the terms overlap.

Open star cluster in the constellation [[Taurus (constellation)|Taurus]], also called the Seven Sisters and Messier 45. It contains over 1,000 stars, and the brightest six or seven are easily visible to the naked eye. At about 444 light-years away, it is the [[Messier object]] nearest to Earth. Its hot blue stars formed within the last 100 million years. Around 2330 BC the cluster marked the [[Equinox|vernal point]], and it marked the start of several ancient calendars. The name probably derives from its role in marking the sailing season in the [[Mediterranean Sea]], and in [[Greek mythology]] it was given to seven divine sisters. Reflection nebulae around its brightest stars are now thought to come from a dust cloud the cluster is passing through, moving at about 18 km/s (11 mi/s) relative to the stars.

First epoch of the [[Quaternary]] period, a geological epoch of repeated glaciations from about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago. Its climate oscillated between cold glacial periods and warmer interglacials, and sea levels dropped as much as 120 m (390 ft) at peak glaciation, exposing the Beringia land bridge. The genus [[Homo]] originated in Africa in the Early Pleistocene. Modern humans spread outside Africa in the Late Pleistocene and reached Australia and the Americas. Most large land animals outside Africa, including [[Mammoth|mammoths]] and [[Mastodon|mastodons]], died out from about 50,000 years ago, probably because of climate change, human expansion or both.

Order of extinct marine reptiles of the [[Mesozoic]] era, with four long flippers and a short tail. Plesiosaurs first appeared in the latest [[Triassic]], about 203 million years ago, became especially common in the [[Jurassic]], and disappeared in the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event|Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction]] about 66 million years ago. Their broad, flat bodies were powered by flippers driven by strong muscles. Plesiosauromorphs had long necks and small heads and caught small animals, while pliosauromorphs had short necks, large heads and were [[Apex predator|apex predators]] that hunted large prey. Plesiosaurs breathed air, bore live young and inhabited oceans worldwide. More than a hundred valid species have been described, and they were not dinosaurs.

Edible fungus, known as the oyster mushroom, of temperate and subtropical forests worldwide. Its common names include gray oyster mushroom, oyster fungus and pearl oyster mushroom. The fan- or oyster-shaped cap is 2–30 cm (1–12 in) wide and white to gray or brown. Its Latin name *ostreatus* refers to the cap's resemblance to a bivalve. It is a white-rot decomposer of dead wood, especially beech and other deciduous trees, and it is absent from the Pacific Northwest of [[North America]]. The mushroom traps and digests [[Nematode|nematodes]], which probably supplies it with [[Nitrogen]]. Commercial cultivation began in Germany during World War I, and it is now grown worldwide for food.

Roman author, naturalist and military commander of the early [[Roman Empire]]. He wrote the encyclopedic *Naturalis Historia* (*Natural History*), a 37-volume work on the natural world and human knowledge that became an editorial model for [[Encyclopedia|encyclopedias]]. He served as a naval and army commander and procurator, and he was a friend of Emperor Vespasian. Of his seven works, spanning 102 volumes, only *Natural History* survives. The lost 20-volume *Bella Germaniae* (*Wars of Germania*) was a source for [[Plutarch]], [[Tacitus]] and Suetonius. Pliny died attempting to rescue people during the eruption of [[Mount Vesuvius]]. In his will he adopted his nephew, who became known as Pliny the Younger.

Second epoch of the [[Neogene]] Period, from 5.33 to 2.58 million years ago. It followed the [[Miocene]] and preceded the [[Pleistocene]]. [[Charles Lyell]] named it in 1833, meaning roughly "continuation of the recent," for its largely modern marine mollusc fauna. The climate became cooler, drier and more seasonal, and grasslands spread across continents. Grazing herbivores such as [[Deer]] and [[Camel|camels]] became common, and coral reefs expanded. Early hominins emerged in [[Africa]] toward the epoch's end.

Family of small [[Passerine|passerine]] birds, many called weavers for their intricately woven nests. Members are also known as weaverbirds, weaver finches or bishops. All are native to the Old World, most of them to sub-Saharan [[Africa]], with a few in tropical Asia. The family is believed to have originated in the mid-[[Miocene]] and includes 122 species. Males of many species are brightly colored, usually red or yellow and black. Most weavers breed colonially, and males usually weave the nests, which serve as displays to attract females. Sociable weavers build apartment-house nests in which 100 to 300 pairs have separate chambers. Some species damage crops, notably the red-billed quelea, reputed to be the world's most numerous bird.

Ancient Greek philosopher in Roman Egypt, widely regarded as the founder of Neoplatonism. He studied for eleven years under the self-taught Platonist Ammonius Saccas in [[Alexandria]]. He then joined the expedition of the [[Roman emperor]] Gordian III to Persia, which failed, and afterward taught in Rome. His metaphysics describes three fundamental principles: the One, the Intellect and the Soul. He held that human souls could return to the One through purification, virtue and mystical ecstasy. Porphyry compiled his writings into the *Enneads*, whose ideas influenced Christian, Jewish, Islamic and pagan thinkers and the [[Renaissance]] revival of Platonism. Plotinus distrusted materiality and reportedly refused to have his portrait painted.

Farm implement for loosening or turning soil before sowing or planting. Plows were traditionally drawn by [[Ox|oxen]] and horses, and modern ones by [[Tractor|tractors]]. Turning the topsoil brings nutrients to the surface and buries [[Weed|weeds]] and crop remains. The earliest plows had no wheels, and the Romans called them an *aratrum*. The [[Industrial Revolution]] brought steam engines to pull plows, which were superseded by internal-combustion tractors early in the 20th century. Because of soil damage and [[Erosion|erosion]], many areas now use shallower plowing or other conservation tillage. The plow appears in one of the oldest surviving literary works, a Sumerian poem from the 3rd millennium BC, in which it debates the [[Hoe (tool)|hoe]] over which tool is better.

Fruit of several *Prunus* species in the [[Rosaceae]] family. Plums were probably among the first fruits domesticated by humans, with origins in Eastern Europe, the Caucasus Mountains and [[China]]. Plum remains have been found at [[Neolithic]] sites, and the fruit was brought to Britain from Asia. The fruit is a drupe with firm, juicy flesh, and it can be eaten fresh, dried as prunes, made into jam, or fermented into wine and distilled into brandy. Plum seeds contain amygdalin, a [[Cyanide|cyanide]]-like poison. Plum cultivation in [[Andalusia]], Spain, was documented in a 12th-century agricultural work. In 2023 China produced 55% of the world's plums, and Japanese or Chinese plums dominate the fresh-fruit market.

System of pipes, valves, fixtures and tanks that conveys fluids, mainly water, for supply, heating and waste removal. The word derives from the Latin *plumbum* (lead), because the first effective pipes in the [[Roman Empire]] were made of lead. Plumbing has ancient roots: the Mesopotamians introduced clay sewer pipes around 4000 BCE, and copper piping appeared in Egypt by 2400 BCE. The city of [[Uruk]] has the oldest known brick latrines, from about 3200 BCE. After the fall of Rome, water supply and sanitation stagnated for well over 1,000 years. In the 1800s, public health authorities pressed for waste disposal systems to control [[Epidemic|epidemics]]. Galvanized iron was common in the United States from the late 1800s until about 1960, after which copper took over. Lead use for drinking water declined sharply after [[World War II]].

Greek and later Roman Middle Platonist philosopher, biographer and essayist, and priest at the Temple of [[Apollo]] in Delphi. He is known for the *Parallel Lives*, paired biographies of illustrious Greeks and Romans such as [[Alexander the Great]] and [[Julius Caesar]], and for the *Moralia*, a collection of essays and speeches. Born in Chaeronea, Boeotia, he studied mathematics and philosophy in Athens and served as a magistrate at home. From c. AD 95 he was one of two priests at the Delphic sanctuary, and he helped revive its shrines. He received Roman citizenship and was on familiar terms with Roman nobles. According to a later historian, Emperor [[Hadrian]] appointed him nominal procurator of Achaea. His writings influenced Renaissance humanism.

Dwarf planet in the [[Kuiper belt]] beyond [[Neptune]], the largest known [[Trans-Neptunian object|trans-Neptunian object]] by volume. Clyde W. Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930 at Lowell Observatory in [[Arizona]], where it was immediately hailed as the ninth planet. Its small size and the discovery of other objects, notably the more massive [[Eris (dwarf planet)|Eris]] in 2005, led the International Astronomical Union to exclude it from the definition of planet in 2006. Pluto is made of ice and rock, with about one-sixth the mass of the [[Moon]] and one-third of its volume. Its largest moon, [[Charon (moon)|Charon]], is just over half Pluto's diameter, and the two orbit a common center of mass. [[New Horizons]] flew past Pluto on July 14, 2015, and made detailed measurements.

[[Chemical element]] with atomic number 94 and symbol Pu, a radioactive [[Actinide|actinide]] metal. It is silvery-gray, tarnishes in air and forms a powder that can ignite spontaneously. Because it is radioactive and can accumulate in bone, it is dangerous to handle. It was first synthesized in late 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley, by bombarding uranium with deuterons, and it was named after [[Pluto]], since uranium and neptunium had been named after Uranus and Neptune. Plutonium-239 and plutonium-241 are fissile, so they are used in [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]] and [[Nuclear reactor|reactors]]. Plutonium-238 generates heat for radioisotope generators that power some spacecraft. Producing plutonium in quantity was a major part of the [[Manhattan Project]] during [[World War II]], and plutonium cores were used in the bombing of [[Nagasaki]].

Large family of [[Monocotyledon|monocotyledonous]] flowering plants, commonly known as the true grasses. It includes the [[Cereal|cereal]] grasses, [[Bamboo]], and the grasses of natural [[Grassland]] and lawns. With around 780 genera and 12,000 species, it is the fifth-largest plant family. It is the most economically important plant family, supplying staple foods such as [[Wheat]], [[Rice]], [[Maize]], oats, [[Barley]] and millet, as well as feed for meat-producing animals. Through direct consumption, rice provides 20% of dietary energy, wheat 19% and maize 5%. Grasslands dominated by grasses are estimated to cover 40.5% of Earth's land area, excluding Greenland and Antarctica. Grass leaves grow from their base, an adaptation to grazing.

Powhatan woman notable for her association with the English colonial settlement at [[Jamestown]], [[Virginia]]. She was the daughter of Wahunsenacawh, leader of the Powhatan Confederacy. English colonists captured her in 1613, and she was baptized as Rebecca. In April 1614 she married the [[Tobacco|tobacco]] planter John Rolfe, and they had a son, Thomas. In 1616 she visited [[London]], where she was presented to English society to stimulate investment in Jamestown. She died at Gravesend in [[Kent]], England, before returning to Virginia. Many stories about her, including those told by John Smith, have been romanticized or disputed.

Episodic series of digital audio or video programs distributed over the [[Internet]] for download or streaming. Podcasts usually feature one or more recurring hosts discussing a topic or current event, in formats ranging from scripted productions to improvised conversation. The term combines "iPod" and "broadcast" and was coined in 2004 by journalist Ben Hammersley, writing for [[The Guardian]]. Episodes are delivered to subscribers through RSS feeds and distributed to services such as Apple, Spotify and YouTube. Making a podcast requires only a [[Microphone]], a [[Computer]] or mobile device, and editing software. Many podcasts are free, while others are sponsored by [[Advertising|advertising]] or sold by subscription. In 2025, Bloomberg reported that a billion people watched podcasts on [[YouTube]] each month.

Large genus of [[Conifer|conifers]] of coniferous trees and shrubs, the most numerous and widely distributed genus in the family Podocarpaceae. Species of *Podocarpus* usually grow 1 to 25 m (3 to 82 ft) tall and occasionally reach 40 m (130 ft). Their cones have two to five fused scales that form a fleshy, berry-like receptacle, which attracts birds that eat the cones and disperse the seeds. The genus is native to much of [[Africa]], Asia, [[Australia]], Central and South America and several South Pacific islands, from southern [[Chile]] to Mexico. Podocarpaceae were endemic to the supercontinent Gondwana, which broke up between 105 and 45 million years ago. The cultivar County Park Fire has won the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

Collection of anonymous Old Norse narrative poems in alliterative verse, known as Eddic poems. The Poetic Edda is distinct from the *Prose Edda* of [[Snorri Sturluson]], and its basis is the medieval Icelandic manuscript *Codex Regius*, also called the Elder Edda. Most poems are in *fornyrðislag* ("old story meter"), with about a quarter in *ljóðaháttr* ("song form"). Like most early poetry, they were passed down orally for centuries. Dating is debated. The poem *Atlamál*, which claims a Greenland origin, must date from about 985 or later, when Scandinavians first reached Greenland. The poems include mythological narratives about gods such as Odin and Thor and heroic lays about legendary figures such as Sigurd. Iceland was settled only around 870, so earlier poems most likely originated in [[Scandinavia]].

Violent riot aimed at massacring or expelling an ethnic or religious group. It originally described late 19th- and early 20th-century attacks on Jews in the [[Russian Empire]], such as the 1903 Kishinev pogrom. The most significant pogrom in [[Nazi Germany]] was the 1938 [[Kristallnacht]], in which at least 91 Jews were killed and 1,000 synagogues burned. Notable pogroms of [[World War II]] included the 1941 Farhud in [[Iraq]] and the Iași pogrom in [[Romania]], in which over 13,200 Jews were killed. The 1984 Sikh massacre, in which 3,000 Sikhs were killed, shows that other groups have also been targeted.

Theorem in geometric topology characterizing the three-dimensional sphere. [[Henri Poincaré]] conjectured it in 1904. It concerns closed, connected three-dimensional [[Manifold|manifolds]] with trivial [[Fundamental group|fundamental groups]], meaning every loop can be contracted to a point, and asserts that such a space is homeomorphic to a three-dimensional sphere. Attempts to resolve it drove much progress in geometric topology during the 20th century. Grigori Perelman completed a program built on Richard S. Hamilton's use of Ricci flow, posting papers on arXiv in 2002 and 2003. The journal [[Science (journal)|Science]] named his proof the 2006 Breakthrough of the Year. The Clay Mathematics Institute included the conjecture among its [[Millennium Prize Problems]] and offered Perelman a US$1 million prize in 2010, which he declined, saying Hamilton's contribution was equal to his own.
